title: A Wife, Three Names
sum: The book opens with a heading that dates Hosea by five kings and then with a command that no other prophet received in these words: marry a wife of prostitution and have children of prostitution, because the land is prostituting itself away from the LORD. Hosea does it. Gomer bears a son, a daughter and a second son, and the LORD gives each a name that is a sentence of judgment: Jezreel ("God sows", for the blood spilled there and the house that spilled it), Lo-ruhamah (Not Shown Compassion) and Lo-ammi (Not My People).

The chapter ends in a reversal (1:10-11, Hebrew 2:1-2). The people who were told "You are not my people" are to be called "children of the living God", and the day of Jezreel will be great. The names that close the door at 1:9 are the names that open it again in 2:1 and 2:23.
readings: Read as a real marriage and its children

Hosea marries Gomer, and the three children are born in the order the text gives. The names were given to the children as living sermons, preached each time their names were called. Most modern commentators read the chapter this way, and they differ on what kind of woman Gomer was when Hosea married her.
Read as a vision or a parable

Maimonides and the Targum held that God would not command his prophet to marry a prostitute, so the account is a vision or a story told for its meaning. Some Christian writers have held the same; this site has not checked which, so none is named. The lesson is the same: Israel is the unfaithful wife and God the husband who does not let go.
Read as the first of the book's sign acts

The marriage, like Isaiah's walk and Jeremiah's belt, is a prophet's life used as a message. On this reading it does not matter whether Gomer was a prostitute before or after the wedding, because the point is what the family shows Israel about itself.

views.H: The setting is the late reign of Jeroboam II, when Israel was rich and secure (2 Kings 14:23-29), and the first years after his death. The "blood of Jezreel" goes back about ninety years to Jehu (841 BC), whose house reigned through five kings and ended when Shallum killed Zechariah, Jeroboam's son (2 Kings 15:10). The "bow" of 1:5 and the promise of 1:7 are often read as pointing to Tiglath-pileser's campaign in the north (733-732 BC) and the rescue of Jerusalem in 701 BC; the notes show that the text names neither.
views.C: The heading names four kings of Judah and only one of Israel, which points to a Judean editor after 722 BC. Chapter 1 is in the third person and chapter 3 in the first, so they may come from different hands or different stages. Many scholars regard 1:7 as a Judean addition and 1:10-2:1 as a later hope. The Dead Sea scrolls preserve only parts: 4Q79 (4QXIId) some of 1:6-11 and 4Q82 (4QXIIg) some of 1:10-11. The words that can be read agree with the Masoretic Text, apart from spelling and a few restored words.
views.J: The Talmud (Pesachim 87a-b) takes the marriage as real and plays on the names Gomer and Diblaim. Maimonides (Guide 2.46) counts it a vision; the Targum recasts the opening as a command to prophesy to the people. The haftarah for Bemidbar (the first Torah portion of Numbers), read before Shavuot, begins with 1:10 (Hebrew 2:1), the promise that Israel will be as numerous as the sand.
views.X: Paul reads 1:10 and 2:23 together in Romans 9:25-26 as the calling of Gentiles and Jews into one people of God, and 1 Peter 2:10 echoes the names. Jerome's Commentary on Hosea (about AD 406) reads the book first of Israel's own history and then of Christ and the church, as he does throughout the Twelve.
views.F: Readers who expect a future restoration of Israel point to 1:10-11 as promising a reunited people "gathered together" under "one head" (compare 3:5), and Romans 11:25-27 is often placed beside it. Others read the promise as already begun in the church, or as fulfilled in the return from Babylon.

deep.b:
ChildNameMeaningReversal
Son (1:3-4)Jezreel"God sows"2:22-23, "I will sow her for myself"
Daughter (1:6)Lo-ruhamah"Not Shown Compassion"2:1, 2:23
Son (1:8-9)Lo-ammi"Not My People"1:10; 2:1; 2:23

The names are given by the LORD, in order, with a reason. Each is undone before the second chapter ends. The structure of chapters 1 to 3 is judgment, hope, judgment, hope, as if the prophet could not say one without the other.

The Hebrew Bible puts the two verses 1:10-11 at the start of its chapter 2, so Hebrew 2:1-2 is English 1:10-11 and Hebrew 2:3-25 is English 2:1-23. This book uses English numbers throughout. The same shift happens at 11:12 (Hebrew 12:1) and 13:16 (Hebrew 14:1).

echoes: 2 Kings 9-10; 2 Kings 14:23-29; 2 Kings 15:8-12; Exodus 3:14; Leviticus 26:12; Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10; Genesis 22:17

settings.what: Hosea's marriage and the naming of three children
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to Hosea; Hosea tells it
settings.to: Hosea himself, and through the names the people of the northern kingdom who heard the children called
settings.when: In the long, secure reign of Jeroboam II, or just after it; the order of the births is the order of the text
settings.why: To make the prophet's household a message: the land is prostituting itself, the house of Jehu will fall, the LORD will no longer have compassion on the north, and the covenant formula "I will be your God" is turned around. Each time the children were named in the street, the sentence was heard again.
settings.readers: After 722 BC, readers in Judah could see that the names had come true, and in 1:7 they could see themselves addressed.
views: Gomer was already living outside the law, or became so; the children are named as signs (Wolff, Andersen and Freedman, Stuart).
The marriage is told for its lesson and never happened outside the vision (Maimonides, the Targum).
It happened, but the text does not say what Gomer was or when; the family itself is the message.

settings.what: The promise that reverses the three names
settings.to: The Israelites, and, as it is placed, the readers of the book after the fall of the north
settings.when: Hebrew 2:1-2; the time is not given, and many think the words were added after 722 BC
settings.why: To say, right after the sentences of 1:2-9, that judgment is not the last word: the people will be numerous, gathered, led by one head and called children of God. Knowing that the promise sits directly behind the names makes the harshness of 1:9 a door and not a wall.
settings.readers: Exiles and survivors who knew that "Not My People" had been carried out read here that the name could be changed.

title: The Case Against the Mother
sum: The children are told to take their mother to court. She has chased her lovers and credited them with the grain, wine, oil, wool and flax that came from the LORD, and so he will take it back, strip her bare and stop her festivals. The speech does not soften. It then turns on the word "therefore" (2:14): he will coax her out to the wilderness, speak to her heart, give her vineyards back and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope. She will call him "My husband" and not "My Baal".

The chapter ends in a betrothal with five gifts, righteousness, justice, loyal love, compassion and faithfulness, and a chain of answers from heaven to earth to grain to Jezreel. The names of chapter 1 are all undone: "I will have compassion on Lo-ruhamah, and I will say to Lo-ammi, 'You are my people.'"
readings: Read as the covenant lawsuit it is
The form is a legal case, with charge (2:2-5), sentence (2:6-13) and, uniquely, a turn to reconciliation (2:14-23). The prophets used marriage law because the covenant was a marriage-like bond.
Read as a hard rhetoric about a woman

Feminist critics ask what the picture of a husband stripping and shaming a wife does to its hearers; defenders answer that it is aimed at Israel's men and leaders. The text is both a metaphor and a particular picture, and neither reading cancels the other.

views.H: The details come from the farming year: grain, new wine and oil; wool and flax; vines and fig trees; the festival calendar. The "lovers" are the Baals and the foreign powers. In the years 740 to 732 BC Israel's kings sought help from Assyria and Egypt (5:13; 7:11; 8:9), and Hosea sees the same trust in all of them.
views.C: Scholars divide 2:2-23 into units at 2:2-13 and 2:14-23, and often see 2:14-23 as a later hope or as a rewriting of an earlier salvation word. The sequence of "therefore" at 2:6, 9 and 14 and the shifts between "you" and "she" are noted. The Hebrew has several rare words (nablut, 'etnah, mefatteha), 4Q78, 4Q79 and 4Q82 preserve parts of 2:1-23, with many words restored. The one clear difference is the shorter line in 4Q82 at 2:23 (see the variant). At 2:2 the two scrolls differ from each other and from the Masoretic Text in small details (4Q79 has "lo" where the Masoretic Text has "lo'", "not"); this site has not tried to settle them and relies on none.
views.J: The haftarah for Bemidbar runs from Hosea 2:1 to 2:22 in the Hebrew numbering (English 1:10-2:20). Men say 2:19-20 (Hebrew 2:21-22) as they wind the tefillin strap on the finger, "I will betroth you to myself forever". This site has not checked Rashi, Ibn Ezra or Kimhi on this chapter, so none is attributed a reading.
views.X: Paul uses 2:23 in Romans 9:25 and 1 Peter 2:10 echoes it. Christian commentators from the fathers on have read the betrothal as the union of Christ and the church (compare Ephesians 5:25-32), a reading that grew along with the Song of Songs tradition.
views.F: The promise of safety, the peace with the animals and the betrothal "forever" are often placed in the last days (compare Isaiah 11 and Ezekiel 34:25). Many see a future for ethnic Israel here; others see the church as the bride already betrothed (2 Corinthians 11:2).

deep.b: The chapter has four movements, each introduced by a word of turning. 2:2-5, the charge, ends with the mother's own words ("I am going after my lovers"). 2:6-8, "So look" (laken), blocks her way and shows her coming back out of need. 2:9-13, "So I will take back", takes away the gifts. 2:14-15, "So look" again, is the surprise: after the threats, he courts her. 2:16-23 is the speech of "on that day", three times (2:16, 18, 21). The same word "therefore" that introduced the punishment now introduces the wooing, and the text does not explain why.

Hosea 2 is the passage most often cited in the debate about prophetic marriage metaphors and violence against women (Setel 1985; Weems 1995; Yee 1992). Defenders (Ortlund 1996; Keefe 2001; Kelle 2005; Moughtin-Mumby 2008) argue that the stripping and the court case are rhetorical, that the "mother" is the whole people, that the addressees are the male leaders, and that the chapter ends in her restoration. The Plain English Translation does not soften the Hebrew of 2:3 or 2:10, and it does not read them as a justification for anything. A reader can accept the metaphor's aim and still refuse its picture.

deep.title: The mother, the children and the sequence of names
deep.b: My own observation, built on the text: in chapter 1 the LORD names the children; in 2:1 the children are told to name each other. The naming moves from the prophet to the people. In 2:23 the LORD speaks the names again and the child answers "My God". If the three-step order is deliberate (God names, the people name, God names and the people answer), the chapter can be read as the slow return of a conversation. It overlaps with the common observation that 2:23 reverses 1:9, and it rests only on 1:4-9, 2:1 and 2:23.

echoes: Isaiah 1:2; Jeremiah 2:2; Jeremiah 3:14; Ezekiel 16; Joshua 7:24-26; Exodus 21:10; Romans 9:25; 1 Peter 2:10; Ephesians 5:25-32

settings.to: Israel, the "mother", and the Israelites as her "children"
settings.when: In the years of Israel's wealth and, more likely, of its slide into Assyrian vassalage; the exact date is unknown
settings.why: To charge the nation with giving the LORD's gifts to other gods and allies, and to threaten the withdrawal of everything a husband owed his wife: food, clothing and rights (Exodus 21:10). Knowing that the speech is a legal case, and that its aim is for her to "take her prostitution away" (2:2), changes it from a curse to an ultimatum.
settings.readers: The northern readers who lost their harvest and festivals to Assyria and the Judeans who read it afterward could see the fulfillment and the warning.
views: The words "she is not my wife" are the formula of a divorce, but the "lest" of 2:3 leaves room for return.
The speech uses the shame-and-honor culture of the time to shock its male hearers; its force is rhetorical (Kelle).
The imagery places a husband's violence in God's mouth and a woman without a voice in the accused's place (Setel, Weems, Yee).

settings.what: The wooing, the betrothal and the reversal of the names
settings.to: The same Israel, now addressed as "you" and "her" at once
settings.when: "On that day", an undated future; many scholars place it after 722 BC
settings.why: To answer the sentence of 2:2-13 with a promise: the wilderness becomes a second honeymoon, the Valley of Achor a door, the Baals' names are erased, the beasts and the war end, and the betrothal is for good. Knowing that the promise comes after the threat shows that judgment was never meant to be the end.
settings.readers: Exiles from the north and readers in Judah who had seen the threats fulfilled; the chapter gave them words to hope with.

traditions.q: Who are "Not My People" now? Hosea 2:23 and Romans 9:25-26
views: The Church is the new People of God, made up of Jews and Gentiles (Lumen Gentium 9), and Paul's use of Hosea shows the Gentiles called into that people. The Church also teaches that the Jews remain dear to God because his gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and that they are not rejected or cursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4).

The Church is the continuation and fulfillment of God's people, and the nations are called into it. This card is a short summary from one general introduction (Ware); this site has not checked a Father's comment on Hosea 2:23 or Romans 9:25-26 (for example Chrysostom on Romans) or a liturgical text, so none is quoted. Orthodox teaching on the Jews varies by period and teacher; no single modern statement binds every church.

The Church is the assembly of all believers, Jewish and Gentile, in which the gospel is taught and the sacraments are given (Augsburg Confession VII). The confessions do not comment on Hosea 2:23; this site has not checked Luther on Romans 9, so none of his readings is reported here.

The covenant of grace is one in both testaments, and the people of God are one body (Westminster Confession 7.5-6; Calvin, Institutes 2.10-11). Calvin read "all Israel" in Romans 11:26 as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile together; other Reformed teachers expect a future large-scale turning of the Jews, and the Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 191) prays that the Jews may be called.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article VI) describes the church as a congregation of baptized believers and does not say whether Hosea's promise to the northern tribes belongs to ethnic Israel. Baptists are found among dispensationalists, historic premillennialists and amillennialists, so they differ on whether the promise of 1:10-2:23 is still to be fulfilled for the Jewish people or is fulfilled in the church.
Israel and the church stay distinct. Paul uses Hosea by analogy for Gentiles, but the promise of 1:10-2:23 is for the nation Israel, to be fulfilled when Israel is restored in the last days.

title: Buying Back the Woman
sum: The shortest of the three marriage chapters is told by Hosea himself. The LORD tells him to go again and love a woman who is loved by a companion and keeps committing adultery, as he loves Israel. Hosea buys her for fifteen shekels of silver and a measure and a half of barley, and tells her she will stay with him for many days without prostituting herself or belonging to another man.

The sign act is explained in the next two verses: Israel will stay many days with no king, prince, sacrifice, pillar, ephod or teraphim, and afterward the Israelites will turn back, seek the LORD and "David their king", and come trembling to the LORD and his goodness. The chapter is five verses long and has been argued over more than most chapters in the Bible.
readings: Read as the same woman
Gomer left or was sold into debt or slavery, and Hosea paid to bring her home. The chapter is the sequel to chapter 1: love that goes on after betrayal.
Read as another woman
The text does not call her Gomer, and chapter 3 may be a second sign act, or the same sign act told in the first person. What matters is the shape: the LORD loves the one who does not love him.
Read as a time of probation
The "many days" for the woman and for Israel are the same, a stretch of waiting without the old ways, before a return. The chapter is about that gap.

views.H: The "many days" without king or prince fit the years after 733-722 BC, when Assyria took the north, killed or deposed its last kings and carried its leaders away (2 Kings 15:29; 17:6). The ephod and teraphim belong to the old shrines; the pillar to the Bethel and Gilgal worship Hosea attacks.
views.C: Chapter 3 is in the first person while chapters 1 and 2 are in the third, and it opens with "again". Wolff and others think 3:5 (or "and David their king" and "in the last days") is a Judean addition; others hold that Hosea himself looked toward the reunion of the tribes. The scrolls 4Q78 and 4Q82 preserve parts of this chapter. The transcription of 4Q82 lacks the clause "for me; you must not prostitute yourself" at 3:3 and has a shorter text or a gap at 3:5 (see the variants); it may be damage or skipped words, and this site has not checked the edition.
views.J: The Targum reads "Messiah the son of David" at 3:5. This site has not checked Rashi or Kimhi on the verse. The Talmud tells a long story of Hosea and Gomer (Pesachim 87a-b). The Jewish reading that Israel will wait without kings and sacrifices is felt strongly in the exile.
views.X: Jerome and Cyril take "David their king" as Christ, and many take the "many days" as the whole age of the church during which Israel is without king and temple. The purchase of the woman has been compared to redemption by Christ (1 Corinthians 6:20; 1 Peter 1:18-19).
views.F: For many readers 3:4-5 is a prophecy of Israel's long dispersion and return: no king or temple for "many days", then a seeking of the LORD and David's son in the last days. Dispensationalists point to the present state of Israel; others hold that the chapter's days have been and are fulfilled in the church.

deep.b: Fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley are not the price of a prostitute. Some commentators think they add up to thirty shekels, the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32); some that this was a bride-price or the repayment of a debt to the man who held her. Whether Hosea paid for ownership, for freedom or for a promise, the text is brief: he "bought" her and set the conditions. The Greek says "hired" and gives a jar of wine in place of the second barley.

The list of 3:4 holds three pairs. The state: king and prince. The shrine: sacrifice and pillar. The oracle: ephod and teraphim. Some of these were approved in the law and some were not, which suggests that the point is the absence of every form of rule and worship, good or bad. The text does not call it a punishment; it calls it a time of staying, and then the turning.

echoes: Hosea 1:2-3; Exodus 21:32; Judges 17:5; 1 Samuel 23:6; 2 Samuel 7; 1 Kings 12:16; Jeremiah 30:9; Ezekiel 34:23-24; Ezekiel 37:24

settings.what: Hosea buys back a woman and explains why
settings.by: The LORD, to Hosea, who tells it in the first person
settings.to: Hosea, and through the sign the people of the north
settings.when: After the births of chapter 1, on the usual reading; undated
settings.why: To show that the LORD's love is not cancelled by betrayal: the woman who loves another is bought back, held in a period of waiting and, the sign says, restored. Knowing that the waiting is the point makes the "many days" of 3:3-4 the main message, not an add-on.
settings.readers: Exiles from the north and readers in Judah after 722 BC, who were living in the "many days" the chapter describes.
views: Gomer, sold or in debt, bought back by her husband.
A second sign, not tied to chapter 1.
Chapters 1 and 3 are two accounts of one marriage.

title: No Knowledge of God
sum: A new section begins with a summons: "Listen to the word of the LORD, Israelites." The LORD has a case against the people of the land because there is no faithfulness, no loyal love and no knowledge of God anywhere in it. The crimes are the commandments broken in a heap (4:2), and the land itself mourns, down to the fish.

Then the charge turns on the priests, whose work was to teach (4:4-10): the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, the priests will be rejected, and they feed on the people's sin. The last half (4:11-19) is about the shrines: wine, sticks of wood, the high places under the trees, daughters and brides, and Ephraim "bound up with idols". Judah is warned to stay away from Gilgal and Beth-aven. The Hebrew of this chapter is among the hardest in the book (4:4, 4:18).
readings: Read as an attack on the priests
Everything from 4:4 on has the priests in view. They failed to teach, they profited from the people's sin offerings, and they led the worship that Hosea thinks is a form of prostitution.
Read as a charge against the whole people
The lawsuit of 4:1-3 names everyone in the land, and 4:11-14 speaks to fathers and husbands as much as to priests. The priests are the first accused, not the only ones.

views.H: The northern shrines (Bethel, Gilgal, Dan, and the high places) were served by priests who were not all Levites (1 Kings 12:31). The chapter pictures the festival crowds, the sacred trees, the wine and the sexual practices of the Baal cult as Hosea saw it, in the 750s and 740s BC. The "mourning" of the land may refer to a drought or to the effects of war.
views.C: The key terms ('emet, hesed, da'at 'elohim) reappear in 6:6 and 12:6 and link the book's parts. The Masoretic Text of 4:4, 4:10-11, 4:18 and 4:19 is disputed, and the Greek differs in each. 4Q78 (4QXIIc) preserves parts of 4:1-19, with many words restored (4:1 and 4:11-13 are mostly restored). Where its words can be read they agree with the Masoretic Text, apart from spelling. Some scholars think 4:15 (the warning to Judah) is a Judean addition.
views.J: This site has not checked Rashi, Ibn Ezra or Kimhi on 4:4-10, so none is attributed a reading. The Mishnah teaches that learning is the foundation of piety (Avot 2:5, "an ignorant person cannot be pious"), a rabbinic saying that matches the charge of 4:6.
views.X: Christian preachers and reformers have used 4:6 against ignorant clergy and unlearned congregations, and the charge against the priests has been read as a warning to church leaders who profit from their people's sins. The "spirit of prostitution" has been read as the pull of idolatry in every age.

deep.b: In Hosea knowing God is not having facts about him. The Hebrew da'at is relationship: it stands beside faithfulness and loyal love in 4:1, and 6:6 sets it beside loyal love again. Jeremiah explains it by a king's justice to the poor: "Is this not knowing me?" (Jeremiah 22:16). The priests' failure was in teaching the people the LORD's ways, so that when they asked a stick of wood for an answer (4:12), they had nothing else to ask.

Hosea 4:13-14 is one of the passages used to claim that Baal worship included sexual rites. The words used are "prostitution" (zenut), "shrine women" (qedeshot) and "adultery", but the older picture of temple prostitution as an organized rite is now doubted (Bird; Budin). What the verses certainly say is that the men go to the shrines, that the women are treated as the sinners, and that the LORD reverses the blame (4:14). See the notes at 4:14 and the topic on high places.

echoes: Exodus 20:13-16; Exodus 34:6; Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10; Jeremiah 22:16; Jeremiah 12:4; Malachi 2:7; Romans 1:24; 1 Kings 12:28-33; Amos 4:4; Amos 5:5

settings.what: The LORD's case against the people of the land
settings.to: The Israelites, "those who live in the land"
settings.when: After the marriage chapters, in the last years of Jeroboam II or soon after; the book gives no date
settings.why: To open the second main part of the book with a charge: the three covenant qualities (faithfulness, loyal love, knowledge of God) are missing, and the commandments are broken until the land itself mourns. Knowing that it is a covenant lawsuit makes the creation language a legal sentence and not a poem.
settings.readers: Readers after 722 BC saw in it the reason for the fall; readers in Judah took it as a warning to themselves.

settings.to: The priests of the northern shrines, spoken to as one man ("you"), and the people with them
settings.why: To tell the teachers that their failure is the cause of the people's ruin: they rejected knowledge, they forgot the teaching of God, they feed on the people's sin. Knowing the priests' job (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10) shows the charge is professional: they did not do their work.
settings.readers: Priests in Judah after the north fell, and every later teacher of God's people.

settings.to: The Israelites at the shrines; Judah in 4:15
settings.why: To expose the festival religion as a form of the unfaithfulness Hosea's marriage acted out: the wood and stick for advice, the hill shrines, the women and men, and the oath at Bethel. Knowing the practices explains why the LORD says he will not punish the daughters (4:14): the men, who lead, are the guilty ones.
settings.readers: Later readers who could compare the shrines to what they knew of their own.

title: A Trap, a Moth and a Lion
sum: The charge widens: priests, the people and the royal house are all to hear, because they have been "a trap at Mizpah, a net spread out over Tabor". Ephraim has prostituted itself and cannot turn back, for a spirit of prostitution is inside. They go to seek the LORD with sheep and cattle, and he has pulled away.

Then the alarm sounds in Benjamin (5:8). Judah's princes move boundary markers, Ephraim is crushed, and the LORD says he is a moth to Ephraim and rot to Judah. Ephraim turns to Assyria and King Jareb, who cannot heal him (Judah also sees its wound), and the LORD becomes a lion who tears and carries off. He goes back to his place until they pay for their guilt and seek his face.
readings: Read as the Syro-Ephraimite war

The alarm and the border lines of 5:8-10 are the war of 735-732 BC, when Aram and Israel attacked Judah, Ahaz called on Assyria, and Tiglath-pileser took Damascus and the north (2 Kings 16:5-9; 15:29). In 5:13 Ephraim goes to Assyria and sends to King Jareb, while Judah "saw his sore"; Ahaz's appeal to Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 16:7) is the Judean parallel, but 5:13 does not tell it.
Read as a general judgment
The place names, the trap and the lion do not need a single war. The chapter is the first of several (7, 8, 9, 10) in which Hosea describes a nation caught between foreign powers and its own gods.

views.H: The towns of 5:8 are in Benjamin on the road north of Jerusalem. Albrecht Alt (1919) tied 5:8 to 6:6 to the Syro-Ephraimite war and its aftermath. Menahem paid Assyria a thousand talents (2 Kings 15:19-20) and Hoshea later paid tribute (2 Kings 17:3). 5:13 fits either king's turn to Assyria.
views.C: The Masoretic Text of 5:2 is nearly untranslatable, and the Greek reads it differently (see the variant). Wolff and others take 5:1-7 and 5:8-15 as separate units; some think 5:8-14 is a single oracle written after Judah's gains in 5:10. "King Jareb" (5:13; 10:6) is an old puzzle. The scroll 4Q78 (4QXIIc) preserves only 5:1a.
views.J: Rosh Hashanah 31a uses 5:15 ("I will go away and go back to my place") among the verses for the ten journeys of the Shekhinah, the divine presence, withdrawing step by step until Israel repents, a reading used about the exile.
views.X: Christians have often read 5:14-15 as God's discipline of his own people: the lion who tears is the same God who heals (6:1), and the withdrawal lasts until they seek him.

deep.b: Around 735 BC Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Aram tried to force Ahaz of Judah into an alliance against Assyria. Ahaz appealed to Tiglath-pileser III, who took Damascus (732) and much of the north (2 Kings 15:29; 16:5-9; Isaiah 7). Isaiah told Ahaz not to fear the two "smoldering stumps" (Isaiah 7:4); Hosea says that Assyria cannot heal Ephraim (5:13), and Judah has seen its own wound there too. Whether 5:8-6:6 reflects that war depends on dating, and nothing in the text forces it.

Chapters 4 and 5 turn on the verb "know". The LORD knows Ephraim (5:3); Israel does not know the LORD (5:4); Ephraim does not know that he is going gray (7:9). In 6:3 the people say, "Let us know", and in 6:6 the LORD says what he wants: knowledge of God.

echoes: Judges 5:14; Judges 19; Isaiah 7:1-9; Isaiah 10:28-32; 2 Kings 15:19-20; 2 Kings 16:5-9; Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 32:39; Hosea 13:7-8; Micah 1:3

settings.what: The call to priests, the house of Israel and the royal house
settings.to: Priests, the people and the king's household in the north
settings.when: During the years of Assyrian pressure, about 740-735 BC
settings.why: To name the three groups responsible for the nation's life and tell them that the verdict is on them. Knowing that Mizpah and Tabor were high places where the leaders lured or trapped the people makes the metaphor of a hunter's net a charge of spiritual predation.
settings.readers: Northern survivors who saw the fall, and Judeans who needed the same warning.

settings.what: The alarm in Benjamin and the LORD's withdrawal
settings.to: Benjamin and Ephraim (the alarm); Ephraim and Judah (the moth and lion)
settings.when: Probably during or after the Syro-Ephraimite war (735-732 BC); other dates are proposed
settings.why: To tell both kingdoms that their trust in Assyria is the wrong cure and that God himself is the one afflicting them, until they come back. The shock of 5:14, God as lion, shows how far the covenant lawsuit has gone.
settings.readers: Judeans after 722 BC who saw Israel's fate; readers in the exile who understood "until they seek my face".
views: Alt's thesis: the oracles belong to the war of 735-732 BC.
The towns and nations are typical and the date is open.

title: Come, Let Us Turn Back
sum: A short song of repentance opens the chapter: "Come, let us turn back to the LORD, for it was he who tore us apart, and he will heal us." After two days he will give us life again, on the third day he will raise us up, and he will come like the dawn and like the spring rain. It is one of the most hopeful passages in the book, and it is read in two opposite ways.

The LORD's answer (6:4-6) is a question: "What can I do with you, Ephraim? What can I do with you, Judah? Your loyal love is like a morning cloud." He wants loyal love, not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. The chapter ends with a list of crimes: Adam, Gilead, the priests on the road to Shechem, and a harvest for Judah.
readings: Read as a sincere return
The song is the people's true repentance, and the LORD's questions in 6:4 are a lament over how quickly they slip. The hope of 6:1-3 is real, and it prepares chapter 14.
Read as a shallow return

The song treats God like a healer on call: he tore us, so he will heal us, after two days. The LORD's reply, that their loyalty vanishes like dew, shows that he does not take it as repentance (Wolff and Stuart, among others).
Read as both
The words are right and the heart is not. Hosea 14 gives the repentance words that the LORD does accept.

views.H: The song may be a liturgy used at the northern shrines in a time of distress, perhaps after a defeat in the war with Aram and Assyria. The "two days" and "third day" express hope of quick relief. The crimes in 6:7-9 (Adam, Gilead, Shechem) may refer to known events that we have lost.
views.C: The unit 6:1-3 may be a quoted liturgy or a Judean addition; some scholars suggest it echoes a fertility-cult song of a dying and rising god (an idea Hosea would then be rebuking). The Greek differs at 6:3 and 6:5 (see the variants), 6:7 ("like a man") and 6:8-9. 4Q82 (4QXIIg) preserves parts of 6:3 and 6:8-11, with many words restored (a single letter of 6:4 survives).
views.J: The Targum reads 6:2 of the resurrection of the dead, and Genesis Rabbah 56:1 counts the "third day" of Hosea among the great third days of Scripture. This site has not checked Rashi or Kimhi on 6:3. After the Temple fell, Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4 has Yochanan ben Zakkai console Rabbi Joshua with Hosea 6:6: deeds of loving kindness atone as sacrifice did.
views.X: Early Christian writers such as Jerome and Cyril of Alexandria read 6:2 of Christ's resurrection on the third day. Jesus quotes 6:6 twice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7), and Paul says Christ rose on the third day "according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:4). This site has not checked Calvin on 6:2, so no reading of his is reported.
views.F: Readers who see a future for Israel read 6:1-3 as the nation's last turning, with the rain and dawn of the end times (Joel 2:23; Zechariah 10:1). Many hold that 6:2 anticipates the resurrection of the dead at the end (Daniel 12:2).

deep.b: The chapter has three voices. In 6:1-3 the people speak, using "we". In 6:4-6 the LORD answers in the first person. In 6:7-11 the prophet or the LORD lists crimes. The line between the song and the answer is the main reading decision, because the same words ("turn back", "know", "dawn", "rain") are used in both. The connection to 5:15, where the LORD says he will go away until they seek his face, shows that the song may be that seeking, and that the answer in 6:4 is the LORD's verdict on it.

deep.title: The song and the answer share their words
deep.b: My own observation: the people's song and the LORD's reply use the same images in opposite ways. The people say that the LORD will come "like the dawn" (6:3), and the LORD says their love is a "morning cloud" and early dew (6:4). The people say he will come "like the rain" that waters the land, and the LORD says he wants loyal love and knowledge (6:6). The reply can be read as taking their own pictures and turning them around: if he is the dawn, they are the cloud that dawn burns off. This overlaps with Stuart's and Wolff's reading of the song as shallow, and rests on 6:3-4 only.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:39; Genesis 22:4; Exodus 19:16; 1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 1:11-17; Micah 6:6-8; Ezekiel 37; Jeremiah 3:22; Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7; Luke 24:46; 1 Corinthians 15:4

settings.by: The people (or their leaders), quoted by Hosea
settings.when: After the withdrawal of 5:15, likely in a time of distress
settings.why: To say what the people said they would do when God hurt them: return, because he heals. Knowing the setting (a liturgy of need) shows why the LORD's next words are not praise.
settings.readers: Readers in exile who needed words for returning, and who could compare these to the repentance of chapter 14.
views: The words are good, and God's reply is lament.
The words are polite but self-serving; God's reply rejects them.

settings.what: The LORD's answer and the list of crimes
settings.when: Following the song, in the same distress
settings.why: To ask what he can do with a people whose loyalty disappears with the morning, to state what he wants (6:6), and to list the broken covenant at Adam, Gilead and Shechem. The famous line about sacrifice is a judgment on how the cult has been used, not a ban on it.
settings.readers: Priests and teachers who read the line against empty ritual (Matthew 12:7), and later readers who recognized themselves in the morning cloud.

traditions.q: Does Hosea 6:2 speak of Christ's resurrection on the third day?
views: The Church professes that Christ rose "on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures" (Catechism §§638-658) without naming Hosea. The Catechism's account of the senses of Scripture (§§115-119) would allow a spiritual reading of 6:2 of Christ alongside the literal sense, the people's restoration; that is an inference from the Catechism, not a Church statement on Hosea 6:2. Jerome reads 6:2 of Christ.

Cyril of Alexandria takes 6:2 of Christ. The Orthodox Church reads the "third day" texts in the light of Pascha, but this site has not checked a Father's or a liturgical text for Hosea 6:2 beyond Cyril and a general introduction (Ware), and the Church does not treat a single Old Testament text as the proof of the resurrection.

The Reformed confessions say that Christ rose on the third day (Westminster Confession 8.4) and do not tie it to Hosea 6:2. Reformed commentators are not reported here: this site has not checked Calvin on the verse, so no reading of his is given.

Commentaries such as Stuart's, Garrett's and Hubbard's read 6:1-3 as the people's hopeful, perhaps shallow, words about national revival and do not take them as a direct prediction of Christ's rising; some add that the third-day pattern prepares for it.

traditions.q: If God wants "loyal love, not sacrifice", what of the Mass and the Lord's Supper?
views: The Mass is not a new sacrifice but the one sacrifice of Christ made present in a memorial, and offering it is itself an act of the Church's love and mercy (Catechism §§1362-1367; Council of Trent, session 22). Prophets such as Hosea judge sacrifice without love and do not abolish worship.
The Divine Liturgy is a "bloodless sacrifice" offered for all, and sacrifice and mercy belong together. The prophets' warning is against ritual used to hide injustice.

The Mass is not a sacrifice that earns forgiveness; the only sacrifices of the church are praise, thanks and a life of love. The Lutheran confessions use the prophets' words against the idea that a priest's work can pay for sin (Apology of the Augsburg Confession XXIV).

Christ's sacrifice was once and cannot be repeated, and the Lord's Supper is a sacrament in which Christ is not offered up; the Westminster Confession (29.2) calls the Mass contrary to this. The believer's own sacrifices are praise and mercy (Hebrews 13:15-16).

The Lord's Supper is an ordinance that remembers Christ's once-for-all death; it is not a sacrifice. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article VII) describes it as a symbolic act of obedience. Hosea's line is read as a call to love over ritual.

title: A Flat Loaf Nobody Turned
sum: Each time the LORD tries to heal Israel, the guilt of Ephraim and the evil of Samaria come to light: lies, thieves and raiders in the street, and a court that is made glad by evil. The next verses turn on one picture: an oven (7:4-7). The people are adulterers burning like an oven that the baker leaves to heat while the dough rises, their hearts banked all night and ablaze at dawn, and they eat up their own rulers. The kings fall, and none of them calls on the LORD.

The second half (7:8-16) gives Ephraim more pictures: a flat loaf that nobody turned over, a man going gray without noticing, a silly dove flapping between Egypt and Assyria, a bird caught in a net and a slack bow. The LORD would redeem them, but they tell lies about him; they wail on their beds and do not cry to him; they turn, but not upward.
readings: Read as a portrait of the last kings of Israel
After Jeroboam II, four kings were killed by their successors (2 Kings 15). The oven, the drunken king's day and the falling kings are the coups. Hosea names the politics and the plots.
Read as a general portrait of a nation without a center
The images (oven, loaf, dove, bow) are not tied to one event. They describe a people mixed with others, gray with unnoticed weakness, going from power to power.

views.H: The coups of 2 Kings 15 are the clearest background: Shallum killed Zechariah (about 752), Menahem killed Shallum, Pekah killed Pekahiah (about 740 on one chronology, about 735 on another), Hoshea killed Pekah (about 732). Menahem paid tribute to Assyria (738), and Hoshea sent to Egypt's king So and stopped paying (2 Kings 17:4). Hosea's "Egypt" and "Assyria" are the two great powers the last kings tried to play.
views.C: 7:4-7 is the worst Hebrew in the chapter, and the oven image is difficult in several places ("baker" or "anger" at 7:6, the verb of 7:5, the sense of 7:4). 7:14 and 7:16 have Greek variants of weight. 4Q82 (4QXIIg) preserves parts of 7:1 and 7:12-16, and 4Q78 (4QXIIc) parts of 7:12-13, with many words restored; where they can be read they agree with the Masoretic Text in the main. No scroll preserves 7:4-7.
views.J: This site has not checked the classical Jewish commentators on this chapter, so none is attributed a reading.
views.X: Christian preachers have used the unturned loaf for half-hearted faith and the silly dove against trusting worldly powers over God.

The figures of Kings do not add up to the known dates without help (see the topic on regnal chronology), and Pekah's twenty years are widely thought to overlap his rivals' reigns.

The oven is clay, built like a pot, and was heated by burning wood inside it; the baker slapped the dough on the hot wall. The prophet uses the oven for three things: the plotters' hearts burning (7:4, 6), the heat of anger or wine, and the way it burns the rulers (7:7). Because the text is uncertain, it is safest to say that the oven is a picture of plotting that smolders and flares.

echoes: 2 Kings 15:8-30; 2 Kings 17:3-6; Psalm 78:57; Psalm 106:35; Deuteronomy 7:8; Hosea 5:13; Hosea 8:9; Hosea 11:5; Hosea 12:1

settings.what: Ephraim's crimes and the plots of the court
settings.to: The leaders and people of Samaria, the royal court
settings.when: In the years of the coups, 752 to about 732 BC
settings.why: To say that the LORD's attempts to heal the nation are met with fresh crimes, and that the court makes itself glad over wickedness. Knowing the history of the murdered kings in 2 Kings 15 makes the oven and the fallen kings concrete.
settings.readers: Judeans after 722 BC could read their northern neighbor's fall in the oven's fire.

settings.when: During the years of Assyrian vassalage and the appeals to Egypt, about 740-725 BC
settings.why: To show a nation mixed with others, weak without knowing it, flying to Egypt or Assyria like a dove, and turning from the LORD. Knowing how Menahem and Hoshea sent tribute and messengers makes the pictures of the loaf, the gray hairs and the dove into diplomacy.
settings.readers: Readers in exile, who knew what the net had caught.
